title: Hypokalaemia (adult)
subject: nephrology
summary: Grade severity, check magnesium, replace orally when possible and give IV potassium chloride for severe, symptomatic or ECG-affected cases at no more than 10 mmol/h and 40 mmol/L peripherally, while treating the cause.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Severity: mild 3.0 to 3.4 mmol/L, moderate 2.5 to 2.9 mmol/L, severe below 2.5 mmol/L.
Symptoms: weakness, cramps, constipation, ileus, flaccid paralysis including respiratory muscles, rhabdomyolysis and arrhythmias.
ECG: flat or inverted T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves. Arrhythmia risk is higher with ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, LVH and digoxin.
Causes, GI and intake: diarrhoea, vomiting, laxative use, fistulae, poor intake. Shift into cells: insulin, beta-agonists, alkalosis, refeeding, thyrotoxic or familial periodic paralysis.
Causes, renal losses: loop and thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, renal tubular acidosis, Gitelman or Bartter syndrome, amphotericin B, aminoglycosides and hypomagnesaemia.

sections.title: Initial assessment
items: Check magnesium, phosphate, creatinine, glucose, bicarbonate and a 12-lead ECG. Hypokalaemia is hard to correct until hypomagnesaemia is corrected.
Give IV potassium for severe hypokalaemia (below 2.5 mmol/L), symptoms, ECG changes or arrhythmia, or when the oral route is not possible.
Paralysis, respiratory weakness or arrhythmia: monitored bed with continuous ECG and assessment of ventilation.
Identify and stop or reduce the cause where possible before relying on supplements alone.

sections.title: Oral replacement
items: Mild: potassium chloride 24 mmol orally two to three times daily (NHS SPS).
Moderate and asymptomatic: potassium chloride 24 to 36 mmol orally three to four times daily.
Give with or after food to reduce gastric irritation; liquid or effervescent preparations are preferred to slow-release tablets.
Recheck potassium within 1 to 3 days and continue until stable in the reference range.
Ongoing diuretic-induced loss: consider adding amiloride or spironolactone, or an ACE inhibitor or ARB where indicated, with potassium monitoring.

sections.title: IV replacement
items: Use premixed potassium chloride bags where possible (20 to 40 mmol/L in 0.9% saline). Avoid glucose-containing diluents initially because glucose lowers potassium further.
Potassium 2.5 to 3.4 mmol/L and unable to take oral: 20 to 40 mmol KCl in 1 L 0.9% saline over at least 8 hours.
Below 2.5 mmol/L or symptomatic: 40 mmol KCl in 1 L 0.9% saline over 6 hours, then recheck.
Maximum peripheral concentration 40 mmol/L. Maximum routine rate 10 mmol/h; up to 20 mmol/h only in emergencies for short periods with continuous ECG monitoring, preferably via a central line.
Maximum 2 to 3 mmol/kg in 24 hours with normal renal function; use lower doses and close monitoring in renal impairment.
In India, KCl 15% ampoules (10 mL = 20 mmol) must always be diluted in the bag and mixed thoroughly; never give as an IV push or bolus.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Recheck potassium about 6 hours after each infusion for severe hypokalaemia, and within 24 hours for milder cases on IV therapy.
Continuous ECG with emergency rates, existing cardiac disease or digoxin therapy.
Check the cannula site for pain, phlebitis and extravasation.
Monitor magnesium and acid-base: persistent metabolic alkalosis suggests ongoing chloride and potassium depletion.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Thyrotoxic or familial periodic paralysis: potassium shifts back out of cells as the attack ends, so use modest doses and monitor closely for rebound hyperkalaemia. Treat thyrotoxicosis.
DKA and HHS: follow the DKA protocol; potassium is added to IV fluids and insulin is delayed when potassium is low.
Renal impairment: replace with caution, at lower doses, with frequent monitoring and renal advice.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Not checking or correcting magnesium, so potassium stays low.
Diluting potassium in 5% dextrose, which can lower potassium further.
Undiluted concentrated KCl given IV is fatal; keep concentrated ampoules controlled.
Overshooting to hyperkalaemia in renal impairment, periodic paralysis, or when the cause (insulin, beta-agonist) is withdrawn.

drugs.name: Potassium chloride IV
drugs.dose: 20 to 40 mmol in 1 L 0.9% saline; 40 mmol over 6 hours if below 2.5 mmol/L
drugs.notes: Max 40 mmol/L peripherally; max 10 mmol/h routinely (20 mmol/h in emergencies with ECG monitoring); max 2 to 3 mmol/kg/day.

drugs.name: Potassium chloride oral
drugs.dose: Mild: 24 mmol two to three times daily. Moderate: 24 to 36 mmol three to four times daily
drugs.notes: Take with food; recheck within 1 to 3 days.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulphate IV
drugs.dose: If magnesium is low: see Hypomagnesaemia protocol
